## Objectives {.unnumbered}

This lab accompanies the Week 5 notes, [*Data Wrangling II - Joins, Strings and Dates*](https://soton-fds.github.io/week05.html).

- Be able to merge datasets using `dplyr` `join` functions.
- Be able to clean and manipulate strings using `stringr`.
- Be able to parse and work with date / time variables using `lubridate`.

When you have finished the lab, there are more questions on the same data in `lab_05_practice.qmd`.

### Task 1: Joining Data

In the directory `data/simpsons` there are four CSV files taken (and lightly sanitised) from [Kaggle](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/prashant111/the-simpsons-dataset/data).
Note that some columns have been dropped from `simpsons_script_lines` to make the exercise more interesting.

- [ ] Load all four of the files

::: {.solution}
```{r}
simpsons_characters <- read_csv("data/simpsons/simpsons_characters.csv")
simpsons_episodes <- read_csv("data/simpsons/simpsons_episodes.csv")
simpsons_locations <- read_csv("data/simpsons/simpsons_locations.csv")
simpsons_script_lines <- read_csv("data/simpsons/simpsons_script_lines.csv")
```
:::

- [ ] Before joining anything, look at the first few rows of each table. What does one row of each table represent? Which columns link the tables together, and would you describe each link as one-to-one, one-to-many or many-to-many?

::: {.solution}
```{r}
simpsons_characters |> head()
simpsons_episodes |> head()
simpsons_locations |> head()
simpsons_script_lines |> head()
```
:::


Answer the following research questions using `join` functions.
(Make sure your outputs print e.g. location or character names, not just IDs).

- [ ] Which character and location pairs have the most lines?
- [ ] Which episodes feature the most characters? (Hint: look at the `n_distinct` function. Is every script line spoken by a character?)

::: {.solution}
```{r}
location_lines <- inner_join(simpsons_script_lines, simpsons_locations, by=c("location_id" = "id"))
location_lines_characters <- inner_join(location_lines, simpsons_characters, by=c("character_id" = "id"))
location_lines_characters |> head()
```
:::

### Task 1b: Choosing a Join

All of the joins in Task 1 were inner joins, which keep only the rows that have a match in *both* tables.
In this task we look at what that throws away.

- [ ] Join `simpsons_script_lines` to `simpsons_locations`, once with `inner_join` and once with `left_join`. How many rows does each result have? Why are they different?
- [ ] Look at some of the rows that appear in the `left_join` result but not the `inner_join` one. What do they have in common?
- [ ] Which episodes in `simpsons_episodes` have no script lines at all? (Hint: see "Other Types of Join" in the Week 5 notes.) Is there a pattern?
- [ ] In Task 1, we used `inner_join` to find which character and location pairs have the most lines. Was that the right choice?

::: {.solution}

:::

### Task 2: String Processing

Answer the following research questions:

- [ ] Which episode has the longest line (in terms of `spoken_words`)?
- [ ] Print that line in full (e.g. with `cat`). Does it look like a single line of dialogue? Find the same line in the raw CSV file: what do you think has gone wrong?
- [ ] How many values of `spoken_words` have this problem? Remove them, and find the longest line again. (Hint: each row of a CSV file ends with a *newline* character, which `R` writes as `"\n"`. You can search for it with `str_detect` like any other text.)
- [ ] In how many episodes are donuts / doughnuts mentioned? (Hint: be careful about capitalisation.)

::: {.solution}

:::

### Task 3a: Parsing Dates

The table below contains the original air dates of four episodes from the first season of The Simpsons, written in several different ways.

```{r}
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)
first_episodes <- tibble(
    title = c("Simpsons Roasting on an Open Fire", "Bart the Genius", "Bart the General", "Moaning Lisa"),
    uk_date = c("17/12/1989", "14/01/1990", "04/02/1990", "11/02/1990"),
    us_date = c("12/17/1989", "01/14/1990", "02/04/1990", "02/11/1990"),
    long_date = c("December 17, 1989", "January 14, 1990", "February 4, 1990", "February 11, 1990"),
    excel_date = c(32859, 32887, 32908, 32915)
)
first_episodes
```

- [ ] Convert each of `uk_date`, `us_date` and `long_date` into a date, using `lubridate`. Check that all three give the same dates.
- [ ] What happens if you use the wrong function, for example `dmy` on `us_date`? Which dates fail to parse, and which are wrong without any warning?
- [ ] `excel_date` contains the same dates stored as Excel date numbers. Convert these into dates too. (Hint: see the Week 5 notes.)

::: {.solution}

:::

### Task 3b: Date Processing

The next dataset contains information about all stocks in the S&P 500, summarised by day, between 2013 and 2018.
It was taken from [Kaggle](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/camnugent/sandp500?select=all_stocks_5yr.csv)

```{r}
#| message: false
stock_data <- read_csv("data/all_stocks_5yr.csv")
head(stock_data)
```

It has the following columns:

- `date`: The date the record was taken.
- `open`: The price of the stock when the market opened.
- `high`: The highest price in that day.
- `low`: The lowest price in that day.
- `close`: The price of the stock when the market closed.
- `volume`: The amount traded in that day.
- `Name`: The stock's ticker symbol, a short code such as `AAL`, `GOOGL` or `BRK.B`.

- [ ] The column names are not consistently formatted: one of them starts with a capital letter. Use `clean_names` to fix this, and check the new column names.

::: {.solution}

:::

Answer the following research questions:

- [ ] Using the `yday` function, find which day of the year has the lowest trading volume on average.
- [ ] Is a given `yday` always the same date? Compare `yday` for 24 December 2015 and 24 December 2016. Then redo the previous question, grouping by month and day instead.
- [ ] Why might this day have such a low trading volume?

::: {.solution}

:::
